decks.title: Outcomes of Democracy — Part 1: Government and the economy
goals: Assess democracy against the outcome of accountable, responsive and legitimate government
Explain transparency and why democratic decisions take time
Interpret evidence on economic growth under democracies and dictatorships
Evaluate the record of democracies on inequality and poverty

slides.heading: Outcomes of Democracy
slides.body_md: We prefer democracy. But what does it actually deliver, and where does it fall short?

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: how to judge democracy fairly, accountable and legitimate government, economic growth, and inequality and poverty
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Almost every country today calls itself a democracy, and most people say they prefer it. But preference is not proof. In this chapter we act like fair judges. We ask what outcomes we can reasonably expect from democracy, and we check its record with evidence, giving credit where it is due and admitting where it falls short.

slides.heading: Judging democracy fairly
slides.body_md: Democracy creates **conditions** for good outcomes; citizens must still **use** them.

rows: Expect democracy to solve every problem
Ask what democracy can reasonably be expected to produce
Blame democracy for everything that goes wrong
Compare democracies with non-democracies on the same outcome
Look at accountability, fairness, dignity and growth together

visual.alt: Table contrasting unfair ways of judging democracy, such as expecting it to solve every problem, with fair ways, such as comparing democracies with non-democracies on the same outcomes

slides.narration: Here is a common mistake: we expect democracy to fix every problem, and when it does not, we call it a failure. A fair judge asks two questions. What can democracy reasonably be expected to produce? And does it do better or worse than other forms of government on the same outcome? Democracy is not a magic wand. It gives citizens tools, and the results depend on how they are used.

slides.heading: The most basic outcome

nodes.label: Accountable: answers to citizens, can be voted out
Responsive: reacts to people's needs and demands
Legitimate: accepted as the people's own government

visual.alt: Tree of the most basic outcome of democracy: a government that is accountable, responsive and legitimate

slides.narration: What is the most basic thing democracy should deliver? A government that is accountable, which means it answers to the people and can be voted out. A government that is responsive, which means it reacts to people's needs. And a government that is legitimate, which means people accept it as their own. Everything else we expect builds on these three.

slides.heading: Quick check: accountability
slides.body_md: A government is **accountable** when…
slides.narration: Think about who the government must answer to.

slides.heading: Transparency: the right to look inside
slides.body_md: **Transparency**: the openness that lets citizens check **how**, and by what procedure, a decision was taken.

nodes.label: Rules and procedures are followed and recorded
Citizens can ask for the records

visual.alt: Flow of transparency: a decision is taken, rules are followed and recorded, citizens can ask for the records, and wrongdoing can be exposed

slides.narration: In a democracy, decisions should follow rules, and citizens should be able to check whether they did. If you want to know why a road contract went to one company, you should be able to see the file. This is called transparency. Laws that give citizens a right to information make it real. Transparency makes corruption harder and builds trust.

slides.heading: Quick check: transparency
slides.body_md: A citizen asks for the official file to see if a road contract followed the rules. This shows…
slides.narration: Which word means being able to look inside how decisions are made?

slides.heading: Slow but sure

rows: Faster: one person or group decides
More likely to work in practice

visual.alt: Table comparing decision-making: democracy is slower but decisions have wider acceptance, work better and can be corrected; dictatorship is faster but decisions may be resented, resisted and rarely corrected

slides.narration: Critics say democracy is slow, and they are right. Every decision has to be discussed and negotiated. A dictator can decide in a day. But look at the other rows. Democratic decisions are accepted by more people, so they usually work better, and mistakes can be corrected. Speed is not the only measure. A slow decision that sticks can beat a quick one that fails.

slides.heading: The record on accountable government

rows: Open public debate on major policies
Found in democracies; dictatorships have no better record on corruption
Often frustrating, but people can protest and vote

visual.alt: Table of the record of democracies: good at regular elections, often weak on open debate, uneven on information, not free of corruption though not worse than non-democracies, and often frustrating on needs though people can protest and vote

slides.narration: Now the honest scorecard. Most democracies are good at holding regular, free elections. They are weaker at open public debate on big policies. Corruption exists in democracies, but there is no evidence that dictatorships are cleaner. And governments often fail to meet people's needs. The difference is that in a democracy, people can complain, protest and vote the government out.

slides.heading: Legitimacy: democracy's own support
slides.body_md: The lasting **support democracy wins** from its own people is itself one of its outcomes.

rows: "Democracy is still the best system for us."
"We will vote them out next time."

visual.alt: Table: people complain that their government is slow, corrupt or ignores them, yet they still say democracy is best and plan to vote the government out

slides.narration: Here is something remarkable. Surveys in many countries, including those of South Asia, find that people complain about their governments but still prefer democracy. A democratic government may be slow, even inefficient, but it is the people's own. They chose it, and they can change it. This acceptance is called legitimacy, and that lasting support is itself one of democracy's outcomes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a 3-mark assessment
slides.body_md: Question: *Assess the record of democracies in producing accountable government.* (3 marks, about 60 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Strength: **regular, free and fair elections**.
Step 2 — Weakness: limited **public debate**; needs often **frustrated**.
Step 3 — Comparison: **corruption** exists, but dictatorships have **no better record** on corruption.
Step 4 — Use the verb: "assess" needs strengths **and** weaknesses.

visual.alt: Marking plan: one mark for a strength, one for a weakness and one for a fair comparison on corruption

slides.narration: When a question says assess, the examiner wants a balanced verdict. Give one clear strength, one clear weakness and a fair comparison. Notice the comparison point: we never claim democracies are free of corruption. We say they are not worse than other systems, and that citizens can expose it. That kind of careful wording earns full marks.

slides.heading: Economic growth: what the evidence says
slides.body_md: Studies of real countries over long periods find dictatorships **slightly** ahead on average growth; the gap is **small**.

visual.alt: Bar chart of imagined figures: 40 democracies grew on average 4.0 per cent a year over 50 years, and 40 dictatorships 4.3 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined study: democracies 4.0, dictatorships 4.3 per cent a year; studies of real countries also find only a small gap.

slides.narration: Do dictatorships grow faster? This chart uses imagined figures, but it mirrors what long-term studies of real countries have found. On average, dictatorships grew a little faster, but the difference is very small: here, three-tenths of a percentage point a year. Within each group, some countries grew fast and others slowly. So the form of government is clearly not the whole story.

slides.heading: What else drives growth?
slides.body_md: So democracy is **no guarantee** of growth, but there is no case for saying it **holds growth back**.

visual.alt: Flow of factors that drive economic growth: size of the population, the global economic situation, cooperation from other countries, and the country's economic priorities

slides.narration: Growth depends on many things: how many people a country has, what is happening in the world economy, whether other countries cooperate, and what a government chooses to prioritise. A democracy with poor priorities may grow slowly; one with good priorities may grow fast. That is why we say democracy does not guarantee growth, but it does not prevent it either.

slides.heading: Quick check: what drives growth?
slides.body_md: Besides the form of government, which of these affects a country's economic growth?
slides.narration: Look for the option that lists real economic forces.

slides.heading: Inequality: equal votes, unequal incomes
slides.body_md: Imagined figures: the richest fifth earns **13 times** the income share of the poorest fifth.

x.label: Fifth of the population (1 poorest to 5 richest), imagined democracy

visual.alt: Bar chart of an imagined democracy: the poorest fifth earns 4 per cent of income, then 8, 13 and 23 per cent, and the richest fifth 52 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined democracy: richest fifth 52%, poorest fifth 4% (13 times as much).

slides.narration: Every citizen has one vote, so politically everyone is equal. But look at incomes in this imagined democracy. The poorest fifth of the people earn just four per cent of all income, while the richest fifth earn more than half. That is thirteen times as much. Many real democracies show this kind of gap. Political equality has not produced economic equality.

slides.heading: The poverty puzzle

nodes.label: The poor are a large share of voters
They could elect governments that put poverty first
Yet poverty persists in many democracies
A real failure that citizens must keep pressing on

visual.alt: Flow of the poverty puzzle: the poor are many voters with one vote each and could elect governments that put poverty first, yet poverty persists, which is a real failure

slides.narration: Here is a puzzle. In many democracies, poor people are a large share of voters. With one person, one vote, they could choose governments that make ending poverty the top priority. Yet poverty persists, and in some places inequality has grown. This is one of democracy's biggest disappointments. Honest answers admit it, and good citizens keep pressing governments to do better.

slides.heading: Quick check: inequality
slides.body_md: Which statement about economic inequality in democracies is correct?
slides.narration: Have equal votes produced equal incomes?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: interpreting a data table
slides.body_md: Question: *Democracies A and C grew 5.1 and 3.2 per cent a year; dictatorships B and D grew 5.4 and 2.9 per cent. Does this support "dictatorships grow faster"?* (2 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — Average each group: democracies (5.1 + 3.2) ÷ 2 → **4.15**; dictatorships (5.4 + 2.9) ÷ 2 → **4.15**.
Step 2 — Look at the spread: the fastest **and** the slowest are both dictatorships.
Step 3 — Conclude: **not supported**; other factors decide growth.

visual.alt: Table: democracies A and C average 4.15 per cent; dictatorships B and D also average 4.15 per cent

slides.narration: Data questions reward two habits. First, compute the group averages and write them down. Here both groups average four point one five. Second, look at the spread inside each group: the fastest and the slowest countries are both dictatorships. So the claim is not supported. Finish with the reason: growth depends on many factors, not just the form of government.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a 5-mark answer on economic outcomes
slides.body_md: Question: *Examine the economic outcomes of democracy.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Growth: dictatorships **slightly** ahead on average; the gap is small.
Step 2 — Other factors: population, world economy, cooperation, priorities.
Step 3 — Inequality: a small rich group takes a large share.
Step 4 — Poverty: persists despite poor voters' numbers, a failure.
Step 5 — Judgement: weakest area, yet democracy still preferable.

visual.alt: Marking plan: growth evidence, other factors, inequality, poverty and a judgement

slides.narration: For examine questions, give evidence and a verdict. Two points on growth, one on inequality, one on poverty and one judgement make five marks. Notice the honest tone: we admit that economic outcomes are democracy's weakest area. Then we explain why, overall, democracy is still preferable. That balance is exactly what examiners look for.

slides.heading: Summary

rows: Basic outcome; good at elections, weaker at debate; legitimacy keeps support high
Citizens can check how decisions were taken; right to information
Slower, but decisions more accepted and effective
Dictatorships slightly ahead on average; small gap; many other factors
Weak record; equal votes have not produced equal incomes

visual.alt: Summary table of part 1: accountable government, transparency, speed of decisions, growth, and inequality and poverty

slides.narration: Let us sum up part one. Democracy's basic outcome is a government that is accountable, responsive and legitimate. Its decisions are slower but more acceptable. Its record is good on elections, weaker on debate and needs. On growth, it is roughly level with dictatorships. On inequality and poverty, its record is weak. Fair judgement means saying all of this, not just part of it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: "Assess" and "examine" need **strengths and weaknesses**.
Never write that democracy is free of corruption; say dictatorships have **no better record** on corruption.
On growth, say the gap is **small** and list **other factors**.
In data questions, **compute averages** and look at the **spread**.
Admit the weak record on **poverty and inequality**; then give a reasoned verdict.
slides.narration: A few tips. When asked to assess or examine, always give both sides. Be careful with corruption: democracies have it, but dictatorships have no better record. On growth, stress that the gap is small and growth has many causes. With data, compute averages and look at the spread. And be honest about poverty and inequality before you give your verdict.

decks.title: Outcomes of Democracy — Part 2: Diversity, dignity and the overall verdict
goals: Explain how democracy accommodates social diversity, and the conditions it needs
Evaluate how democracy promotes the dignity of women and disadvantaged groups
Explain why dissatisfaction can be a sign of democracy's success
Give a balanced overall verdict on the outcomes of democracy

slides.heading: Diversity, dignity and the verdict
slides.body_md: Can people who differ live together as equals? And why do citizens of democracies complain so much?

visual.alt: Route map of part 2: accommodating social diversity, the two conditions, dignity and freedom, why complaints signal success, and the overall verdict
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we judged democracy on government and the economy. Now we turn to society. Can people of different languages, religions and backgrounds live together peacefully and as equals? Does democracy protect the dignity of each person? And why do people in democracies complain so much? By the end, you will be able to give a balanced overall verdict.

slides.heading: Handling differences peacefully
slides.body_md: Group conflicts never vanish for good in any society; democracy is the best way of **managing** them.

nodes.label: Democracy provides rules for negotiation and peaceful competition
Tensions are expressed through debate, elections and courts
Conflicts are less likely to become violent

visual.alt: Flow: groups have different interests; democracy provides rules for negotiation and peaceful competition; tensions are expressed through debate, elections and courts; conflicts are less likely to become violent

slides.narration: Every society has differences and conflicts between groups. No government can make them disappear for ever. What democracy does is provide peaceful ways to handle them: debate, negotiation, elections and courts. When groups can compete fairly for influence, they are less likely to turn to violence. This ability to manage differences peacefully is one of democracy's biggest strengths.

slides.heading: Two conditions for accommodating diversity

rows: The larger group must cooperate with minorities so that government speaks for the whole people
A majority that ignores minorities breeds resentment
Majorities should not be fixed by religion, race or language; every citizen should have a chance to be in a majority on some issue
Sri Lanka: a language majority dominated and conflict followed

visual.alt: Table of two conditions: democracy is not simply majority rule, so the majority must work with minorities; and rule by majority must not become rule by a permanent majority community defined by religion, race or language, as the Sri Lanka example warns

slides.narration: Democracy can accommodate diversity only if two conditions hold. First, it is not simply rule by majority opinion; the majority must work with minorities. Second, the majority must not be a fixed community defined by birth, such as religion or language. Every citizen should have a chance to be part of a majority on some issue. Sri Lanka showed what happens when this condition is broken.

slides.heading: Quick check: majority and minority
slides.body_md: Which condition must hold for democracy to accommodate social diversity?
slides.narration: Is the majority allowed to be a fixed community by birth?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: apply the conditions to a case
slides.body_md: Question: *In an imagined country, the largest language group passes a law that only its language may be used in courts. Which condition is broken, and what might follow?* (3 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — Identify: majority defined by **language** uses power to **exclude**.
Step 2 — Condition broken: rule by majority has become rule by a **majority community**.
Step 3 — Likely result: minorities feel **alienated**; distrust may grow into **conflict**, as in **Sri Lanka**.

rows: Alienation and conflict, as in Sri Lanka

visual.alt: Table: a language majority holds power, breaking the condition against a permanent majority community, with likely alienation and conflict as in Sri Lanka

slides.narration: Here we apply a concept to a new case. First, notice who holds power and how they are defined: by language, which is fixed by birth. That breaks the second condition. Then predict the result using a case you know. Linking the imagined country to Sri Lanka shows the examiner that you can transfer your learning.

slides.heading: Dignity and freedom

rows: Treated as an equal citizen with rights, not a subject
Rights must be used and defended
Equality accepted in principle; laws, courts and votes support their claims
Stronger claim to equal status and opportunity; voice in politics

visual.alt: Table of dignity and freedom: every citizen is treated as an equal with rights; women's claims are supported by law and votes though discrimination continues; disadvantaged castes have a stronger claim to equal status though prejudice persists

slides.narration: Democracy treats every person as an equal citizen with rights, not as a subject who must obey. This has transformed the lives of groups that were long denied respect. Women have used laws, courts and votes to claim equality. Groups once treated as inferior because of caste have gained a stronger claim to equal status. The change is real, but it is not complete.

slides.heading: Quick check: dignity of women
slides.body_md: How has democracy helped improve the dignity of women?
slides.narration: Has discrimination ended, or has something else changed?

slides.heading: From subjects to citizens
slides.body_md: Democracy's deepest change is in **people themselves**.

visual.alt: Table contrasting subjects, who obey, have no say and fear complaining, with citizens, who question rulers, vote and organise, and complain openly

slides.narration: Think about the difference between a subject and a citizen. A subject obeys and stays silent. A citizen questions, votes, organises and demands. Democracy turns people from subjects into citizens. That is why the people of a democracy so often criticise their governments. It is not a sign that democracy has failed. It is a sign that people have learnt to expect more.

slides.heading: Why complaints are a sign of success
slides.body_md: Democracy is a **never-ending** project: as expectations rise, it is judged by **higher standards**.

nodes.label: People gain rights and a voice
Citizens complain when governments fall short

visual.alt: Flow: people gain rights and a voice, some needs are met, expectations rise, citizens complain when governments fall short, and governments are pushed to improve

slides.narration: Here is the cycle. People gain rights. Some of their needs are met. Their expectations rise, so they complain when the government falls short. Those complaints push the government to do better. In this sense, dissatisfaction is evidence that democracy is working. Democracy is never finished. Each generation expects more, and that keeps it moving forward.

slides.heading: Quick check: complaints
slides.body_md: People in a democracy often complain about their government. How can this be seen as a sign of democracy's success?
slides.narration: Would people under a dictatorship dare to complain so openly?

slides.heading: The overall scorecard

rows: About the same; dictatorships slightly ahead on average

visual.alt: Overall scorecard: democracy is clearly better on accountable government and dignity, better on transparency and diversity, about the same on growth, and weak on inequality and poverty

slides.narration: Put everything together. On accountable and legitimate government, dignity and freedom, democracy is clearly better. On transparency and handling diversity, it is better, though uneven. On growth, it is about level with dictatorships. On inequality and poverty, its record is weak. A fair verdict says that democracy is better overall, while admitting where it must improve.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a source on dignity
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *An imagined woman sarpanch from a Scheduled Caste family says her mother could not use the upper well; today she chairs the gram sabha, though some families still avoid her at weddings.*
bullets: Step 1 — (a) "One example of past discrimination" (1): **not allowed to use the upper well**.
Step 2 — (b) "Which arrangement helped her?" (1): **reservation in panchayats**.
Step 3 — (c) "How far has democracy promoted dignity?" (2): **progress** (she leads) + **limits** (social avoidance).

rows: Progress and limits, both from the source

visual.alt: Table: part a past discrimination, part b reservation in local bodies, part c progress and limits from the source

slides.narration: In sources about dignity, look for a before and an after. The well shows the past; chairing the gram sabha shows the present. For how far questions, always give both progress and limits, each with a line from the source. Write respectfully: describe what changed for people, without blaming any community.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the overall verdict (5 marks)
slides.body_md: Question: *"Democracy is better than any other form of government." Evaluate.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Three strengths: accountable and legitimate government; peaceful handling of diversity; dignity and freedom.
Step 2 — One limit: weak record on **inequality and poverty**; decisions can be slow.
Step 3 — Comparison: dictatorships are **not** clearly better on growth.
Step 4 — Verdict: democracy is **better**, but citizens must keep pushing it to improve.

visual.alt: Marking plan: accountability and legitimacy, diversity, dignity, limits weighed, and a reasoned verdict

slides.narration: This is the big evaluation question of the chapter. Give three strengths, one honest limit and a comparison with dictatorships on growth. Then give your verdict in one confident sentence. Notice that a balanced answer is more convincing than a one-sided one. Examiners reward the student who admits the weaknesses and still argues the case clearly.

slides.heading: Quick check: subjects and citizens
slides.body_md: Democracy is said to change people from **subjects** into **citizens**. What does this mean?
slides.narration: What can a citizen do that a subject cannot?

slides.heading: Summary

rows: Democracy manages conflicts peacefully; it cannot remove them for ever
Majority works with minorities; no permanent majority community by birth
Equal citizens; women and disadvantaged castes have stronger claims; change incomplete
Show aware, critical citizens; democracy is a never-ending project
Better overall; weak on inequality and poverty

visual.alt: Summary table of part 2: diversity, the two conditions, dignity, complaints and the overall verdict

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Democracy manages social differences peacefully, provided the majority works with minorities and no community is a permanent majority by birth. It treats people as equal citizens and has strengthened the claims of women and disadvantaged groups, though the change is incomplete. Complaints show citizens expect more. Overall, democracy is better than the alternatives, while it still has much to improve.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **two conditions** for accommodating diversity and link them to **Sri Lanka**.
For dignity, give **progress and limits** together.
Explain why complaints are **evidence that democracy is working**: subjects become citizens.
Final verdicts need **three strengths, one limit, one judgement**.
Write about groups respectfully; describe changes, not blame.
slides.narration: Final tips. Learn the two conditions for accommodating diversity, and use Sri Lanka as your warning example. For dignity, always mention both progress and what remains. Explain why complaints show success. For the big verdict question, use three strengths, one limit and a clear judgement. And whenever you write about women or castes, describe changes respectfully and factually.

notes.title: Outcomes of Democracy — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Judging democracy fairly
sections.body_md: Judge democracy by what it can **reasonably** be expected to deliver, and compare it with **non-democracies** on the same outcome. Democracy creates **conditions** for good outcomes; whether they are achieved depends also on how citizens **use** their rights.

key_terms.definition_md: A result that a form of government can reasonably be expected to produce.

rows: Ask what democracy can reasonably deliver
Weigh accountability, dignity, diversity and growth

visual.alt: Table of unfair and fair ways of judging democracy

sections.heading: 2. Accountable, responsive and legitimate government
sections.body_md:
**Accountable:** the government answers to citizens, who can question it and **vote it out**. Mechanisms: regular, free and fair **elections**; open **public debate**; citizens' **right to information**.

**Transparency:** the openness that lets citizens **check how, and by what procedure,** a decision was taken; it discourages corruption.

**Responsive:** the government reacts to people's **needs and demands**.

**Speed:** democratic decisions involve **deliberation and negotiation**, so they are **slower**, but they are more **acceptable** and more **effective**, and mistakes can be corrected.

**Record:** good on **regular elections**; often weak on **open public debate**; governments often **let people down**; **corruption** exists, but dictatorships have **no better record** on corruption.

**Legitimate:** a democratic government is the **people's own**; it may be slow or inefficient, yet support for democracy stays high (surveys in South Asia and elsewhere). The lasting **support democracy wins** from its own people is itself one of its outcomes.

key_terms.definition_md: A government that must answer to citizens and can be removed by them.
The openness that lets citizens check how, and by what procedure, a government decision was taken.
A government accepted by the people as rightful, because they chose it.

visual.alt: Tree of the basic outcome: accountable, responsive and legitimate government

sections.heading: 3. Economic growth, inequality and poverty
sections.body_md:
**Growth:** studies of many countries over long periods find that dictatorships have had a **slightly higher** average growth rate; the **difference is small**. Growth also depends on **population size**, the **global economic situation**, **cooperation from other countries** and the country's **economic priorities**. So democracy is **no guarantee** of growth, but there is no case for saying it holds growth back. Given its other outcomes, democracy remains **preferable**.

**Inequality:** many democracies show **large and sometimes growing** inequality: a small rich group earns a **very large share** of income, while the poorest earn little. **Political equality** (one person, one vote) has not produced **economic equality**.

**Poverty:** the poor are a **large share of voters**, yet poverty **persists** in many democracies: a real **failure** of democratic governments.

key_terms.definition_md: Large differences in income and wealth between groups in a society.
Every citizen has equal political rights, such as one vote of equal value.

rows: About level; dictatorships slightly ahead on average
Weak: income concentrated at the top
Weak: persists despite poor voters' numbers

visual.alt: Table of democracy's economic record

sections.heading: 4. Social diversity, dignity and freedom
sections.body_md:
**Diversity:** group conflicts never vanish for good in any society. Democracy develops **procedures** for negotiation and **peaceful competition**, so tensions are less likely to turn **violent**. Two conditions:
1. Democracy is **more than winning votes**: the larger group must **cooperate with minorities** so that government speaks for the **whole people**.
2. The majority must not be a **fixed community** defined by religion, race or language; every citizen should have a **chance of being in a majority** at some time. (Warning example: Sri Lanka.)

**Dignity and freedom:** democracy treats every person as an **equal citizen** with rights. **Women** have used democratic rights, laws and courts to claim respect and equality; groups once treated as **inferior by caste** have gained a firmer footing to demand **equal standing and equal chances**. Discrimination has **not ended**, but equality is accepted in **principle**, which gives these claims legal and moral force.

**Expectations:** democracy changes people from **subjects** into **citizens**. As some needs are met, **expectations rise**; citizens complain when governments fall short. Such dissatisfaction is **evidence that democracy is working**, and democracy is a **never-ending** project.

key_terms.definition_md: Making room for different groups so that all can live together as equals.
The respect due to every person as an equal human being and citizen.

rows: Majorities not fixed by religion, race or language

visual.alt: Table of the two conditions for accommodating diversity

visuals.alt: Flow of rising expectations in a democracy

sections.heading: 5. The overall verdict
sections.body_md:
| Outcome | Compared with non-democracies |
|---|---|
| Accountable, legitimate government | Clearly better |
| Transparency | Better, though uneven |
| Economic growth | About the same |
| Inequality and poverty | Weak for democracies too |
| Accommodating diversity | Better |
| Dignity and freedom | Clearly better |

**Verdict:** democracy is **better overall**; its weakest area is **inequality and poverty**, which citizens must keep pressing governments to improve.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that democracies are **free of corruption**: they are not, but dictatorships have **no better record** on corruption.
- Claiming democracies grow **much faster**: the evidence shows a **small** gap the other way, and many other factors matter.
- Calling democracy simply **majority rule**: the majority must work with minorities, and no community should be a permanent majority.
- Treating complaints as proof of **failure**: they show aware, critical **citizens**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points (about 40 words); 3 marks: three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks: five points (about 120 words); "assess", "examine" and "evaluate" need **both sides and a verdict**.
- Data items: compute **averages and gaps**, and look at the **spread** within groups.

Often **high**: a small rich group takes a large share of income.
**One person, one vote** has not produced **equal incomes**.
The poor are **many voters**, yet poverty **persists**: a real failure.
Richest fifth **52%**, poorest **4%** → richest earn **13 times** the share.
**Procedures** for negotiation and peaceful competition; less **violence**.
Not simply **majority rule**: majority must **work with minorities**.
No **permanent majority community** by religion, race or language.
**Sri Lanka**: a language majority dominated; conflict followed.

cards.front_md: Democracy and the dignity of women
cards.back_md: Equality accepted in **principle**; laws, courts, votes support their claims.
Stronger claim to **equal status and opportunity**; prejudice persists in places.
Subjects **obey**; citizens **question, vote and demand**.
They show **aware, critical citizens** with rising **expectations**.
As expectations rise, democracy is judged by **higher standards**.
Better on accountability, diversity and dignity; level on growth; **weak on inequality and poverty**.
Three **strengths**, one **limit**, one **verdict**.
A citizen inspects the **file** on how a contract was awarded.

questions.stem_md: What is the most basic outcome that we can expect from a democracy?

options.text_md: A government that is accountable and responsive to its citizens and legitimate in their eyes
A government that never makes mistakes
The fastest possible economic growth
The end of all social conflict

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: No form of government can promise zero mistakes, the fastest growth or an end to all conflict.
Step 2: What democracy can be expected to produce is a government that answers to the people, responds to their needs and is accepted as their own, so (a).

questions.stem_md: A government is **accountable** when

options.text_md: it takes decisions in secret
citizens can question its decisions and remove it through elections
it is led by the oldest leaders
it never changes its policies

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Accountability means being answerable to the people.
Step 2: Citizens question the government and can vote it out, so (b).

questions.stem_md: A citizen can find out whether a road contract was given according to the rules, by asking for the official file. This shows

options.text_md: majoritarianism
economic growth
transparency in decision-making
a one-party system

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Being able to examine how a decision was taken is transparency.
Step 2: In a democracy, citizens can check whether decisions followed proper procedures, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Democratic decisions often take longer than decisions in a dictatorship. Why is this **not** necessarily a weakness?

options.text_md: Because slow decisions are always better
Because dictators never take decisions
Because democracies do not need to take decisions
Because decisions taken after discussion and negotiation are more likely to be accepted and to work

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Democracy involves deliberation and negotiation, which take time.
Step 2: The result is decisions that more people accept, and that are more effective in practice. So the time cost is often worth it: (d).

questions.stem_md: Which pair best compares decision-making in a democracy and a dictatorship?

options.text_md: Democracy: slower but more acceptable decisions. Dictatorship: faster but often less acceptable decisions.
Democracy: faster and secret. Dictatorship: slower and open.
Both are equally transparent.
Neither takes any decisions.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dictatorships can decide quickly, without consulting anyone.
Step 2: Democracies consult and debate, so they are slower but their decisions carry wider acceptance. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a mechanism by which a democratic government is made accountable to citizens?

options.text_md: Regular, free and fair elections
Banning newspapers
Unlimited terms for the ruler
Secret laws

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Accountability needs ways for citizens to judge and replace rulers.
Step 2: Regular, free and fair elections are the main such mechanism; open debate and the right to information are others. So (a).

questions.stem_md: On which aspect of accountable government do most democracies have a **good** record?

options.text_md: Holding regular and free elections
Holding open public debate on every major policy
Ending corruption completely
Meeting all the needs of the poor

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Most democracies succeed in holding regular, free elections.
Step 2: Their record on open public debate, corruption and meeting people's needs is much weaker. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about corruption is supported by experience?

options.text_md: Democracies are completely free of corruption.
Corruption exists in democracies, but there is no evidence that non-democratic governments are less corrupt.
Only democracies suffer from corruption.
Dictatorships have no corruption because they are strict.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Democracies are not immune to corruption.
Step 2: But dictatorships have no better record on corruption, and in democracies citizens can at least expose it and vote against it. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Why is a democratic government called a **legitimate** government?

options.text_md: Because it is always efficient
Because it is the people's own government, chosen by them
Because it is run by experts
Because it has the strongest army

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Legitimacy means being accepted as rightful by the people.
Step 2: A democratic government is elected by the people and is seen as their own, even when it is slow or inefficient, so (b).

questions.stem_md: An imagined survey finds that most people in five South Asian countries prefer democracy to any other form of government, even though many are unhappy with their own government's work. What does this show?

options.text_md: Democracy has lost all support.
People prefer dictatorship.
The lasting support democracy wins from its own people is itself an outcome of democracy.
People do not care how they are governed.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: People criticise their governments but still prefer democracy.
Step 2: This continuing support is a sign of legitimacy, an outcome of democracy, so (c).

questions.stem_md: A villager learns, through an application to the government office, how much money was spent on her village school. Which feature of accountable government does this reflect?

options.text_md: The right to vote
The rule of the majority community
Citizens' right to information about government decisions
The independence of the judiciary

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: She obtained official information about public spending.
Step 2: That reflects citizens' right to information, one of the means of holding governments accountable, so (c).

questions.stem_md: After floods, a state government quickly changes its plans and sends aid after protests by affected villagers. This shows that the government is

options.text_md: responsive
majoritarian
unaccountable
secretive

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The government reacted to people's needs and demands.
Step 2: That is responsiveness, so (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement fairly describes the record of democracies in responding to people's needs?

options.text_md: Democracies always meet every need of the people.
Democracies never listen to the people.
Democratic governments often let people down and leave many demands unmet, though, unlike non-democracies, they allow these demands to be raised.
Responsiveness has nothing to do with democracy.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The honest verdict is mixed.
Step 2: Democracies often fail many people, but people can at least raise demands, protest and vote, which is not possible under dictatorships. So (c).

questions.stem_md: What does the evidence on economic growth over several decades suggest about democracies and dictatorships?

options.text_md: Democracies always grow twice as fast.
Dictatorships have had a slightly higher growth rate on average, but the difference is small.
Dictatorships always remain poor.
Growth has nothing to do with any factor except the form of government.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Studies of many countries over long periods found a slightly higher average growth rate under dictatorships.
Step 2: The gap is small and the form of government is only one factor, so (b).

questions.stem_md: Besides the form of government, which of these affects a country's economic growth?

options.text_md: Size of the population, the global economic situation, cooperation from other countries and the country's economic priorities
Only the number of political parties
Only the colour of the national flag
Only the number of elections held

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Growth depends on many factors.
Step 2: Population size, the world economy, cooperation from other countries and economic priorities all matter, so (a).

questions.stem_md: If dictatorships grow slightly faster on average, why should we still prefer democracy?

options.text_md: Because democracy guarantees the highest growth
Because the growth gap is small and democracy has many other positive outcomes, such as dignity, freedom and accountability
Because dictatorships cannot exist
Because growth does not matter at all

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The difference in growth is negligible.
Step 2: Democracy offers outcomes such as freedom, dignity and accountable government that dictatorships do not, so (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about economic inequality in democracies is correct?

options.text_md: Democracies have removed all inequality.
Income is equally shared in every democracy.
Only dictatorships have poverty.
Many democracies have large inequalities: a small rich group gets a big share of income, while many remain poor.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Political equality (one person, one vote) has not produced economic equality.
Step 2: In many democracies a small group earns a very large share and the poorest earn very little, so (d).

questions.stem_md: In many democracies the poor are a large share of voters. Why is it surprising that poverty has not been removed?

options.text_md: Because the poor cannot vote
Because parties do not exist
Because poor voters, if they all wanted it, could choose governments that put poverty first
Because the rich do not vote

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: With one person, one vote, a poor majority could in principle make poverty the top priority.
Step 2: That poverty persists anyway is a puzzle and a failure of democracies, so (c).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined study, 40 democracies grew at an average of 4.0 per cent a year over 50 years, and 40 dictatorships at 4.3 per cent. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text_md: Dictatorships are much better for growth.
Democracies cannot grow.
The form of government is the only cause of growth.
The difference is small, so the form of government alone does not decide growth.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The gap is 0.3 percentage points a year, which is small.
Step 2: Many other factors affect growth, so we cannot say democracy holds growth back, (d).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined democracy, the richest 20 per cent of people earn 52 per cent of all income and the poorest 20 per cent earn 4 per cent. How many times the income share of the poorest fifth does the richest fifth earn?

options.text_md: 4 times
8 times
13 times
48 times

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: 52 divided by 4 is 13.
Step 2: The richest fifth earns 13 times the share of the poorest fifth, so (c).

questions.stem_md: "Choosing democracy does not by itself make a country rich." Which statement best supports this?

options.text_md: Some democracies have grown fast and others slowly, because growth also depends on other factors.
All democracies are poor.
All dictatorships are rich.
Democracies do not collect taxes.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Democracies differ widely in growth.
Step 2: Since growth also depends on population, the world economy and priorities, being a democracy does not by itself ensure development, so (a).

questions.stem_md: A democratic government wants to reduce inequality. Which policy is most directly aimed at this?

options.text_md: Cutting all spending on public schools
Raising taxes on the poor
Free school meals and health care paid for by taxes that rise with income
Banning trade unions

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Reducing inequality means shifting resources towards those with less.
Step 2: Public services for all, funded by progressive taxes, do this, so (c).

questions.stem_md: How do democracies usually handle social differences and conflicts?

options.text_md: They develop procedures for peaceful competition, which reduce the chance of conflicts becoming violent.
They ban all differences.
They let the strongest group decide everything.
They ignore all conflicts.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: No society can remove all conflicts between groups.
Step 2: Democracies provide rules for negotiation and competition, so tensions are less likely to explode into violence, (a).

questions.stem_md: Which condition must hold for democracy to accommodate social diversity?

options.text_md: The majority should always be the same community.
Minorities should not take part in government.
The majority should not be a fixed community defined by religion, race or language.
Only one language should be used.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion.
Step 2: The majority must work with minorities, and no community should be a permanent majority by birth, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Why should every citizen have a chance of being in the majority at some time?

options.text_md: So that elections can be cancelled
So that one community can rule permanently
So that minorities can be excluded
So that people are not shut out of power permanently because of the group they were born into

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: If majorities were fixed by birth, some groups would never share power.
Step 2: Changing majorities on different issues keep everyone included, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Which earlier case study shows what can happen when rule by majority becomes rule by a majority community?

options.text_md: Belgium
Sri Lanka
Switzerland
Australia

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In Sri Lanka, the majority community used its majority to dominate, which alienated the Tamil minority.
Step 2: Distrust grew into civil war, so (b). Belgium is the example of accommodation.

questions.stem_md: How has democracy helped improve the dignity of women?

options.text_md: It has ended all discrimination against women.
The principle of equal citizenship has given women's struggles legal and moral support.
It has stopped women from voting.
It has made women's issues private matters.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Discrimination continues, so (a) is false.
Step 2: But once equality is accepted in principle, women can use democratic rights to struggle for respect and equal treatment, so (b).

questions.stem_md: In India, how has democracy affected groups that were once treated as inferior because of caste?

options.text_md: It has strengthened their claim to equal status and opportunity, though discrimination has not fully ended.
It has made their position worse.
It has ended all caste discrimination for ever.
It has had no effect.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Equal rights and the vote have given these groups a stronger claim to dignity.
Step 2: Caste discrimination still exists in some places, so the change is real but incomplete, (a).

questions.stem_md: People in a democracy often complain about their government. How can this be seen as a sign of democracy's success?

options.text_md: It shows that democracy has failed completely.
It shows people are afraid of the government.
It shows that people have become aware and critical citizens who expect more from those in power.
It shows that elections are not held.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Under dictatorship, people may not dare to complain.
Step 2: Complaints show people have moved from being subjects to being citizens with expectations, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Why is democracy described as a "never-ending" project?

options.text_md: Because once people get some benefits, they expect and demand more, so democracy must keep improving
Because elections never take place
Because democracy never makes any progress
Because the Constitution can never be amended

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: As some demands are met, citizens raise new expectations.
Step 2: Democracy is judged against ever higher standards, so it must keep improving, (a).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined democracy, the speakers of the largest language win every election and pass a law that only their language may be used in courts. Which democratic principle is being broken?

options.text_md: Regular elections
Universal adult franchise
Separation of powers
Rule by majority must not become rule by a permanent majority community

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The majority is defined by language and uses power to exclude others.
Step 2: That turns rule by majority into rule by a majority community, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Democracy is said to change people from **subjects** into **citizens**. What does this mean?

options.text_md: People must obey whatever rulers decide.
People gain rights, can question rulers and take part in deciding how they are governed.
People lose the right to vote.
People become government employees.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A subject obeys; a citizen has rights and a say.
Step 2: Democracy gives people rights to question, vote and take part, so (b).

questions.stem_md: Which is the most balanced overall judgement on the outcomes of democracy?

options.text_md: Democracy has solved every problem.
Democracy has failed on every count.
Democracy is clearly better at accountability, dignity and handling diversity, and is not worse at growth, but it has a weak record on inequality and poverty.
Democracy is only about elections.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Weigh each outcome: political, economic, social.
Step 2: Democracy does well on the political and social outcomes, is about level on growth and does poorly on inequality, so (c).

questions.stem_md: In a city council, a ward with a small minority population wins funds for a community hall after its councillors join a broad coalition on a city-wide water plan. This illustrates that in a democracy

options.text_md: minorities can never gain anything
majorities on different issues are formed by changing combinations of groups
only the largest group decides
councils should not discuss water

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The minority ward became part of a majority on one issue.
Step 2: Changing coalitions mean groups are not permanently excluded, so (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Decisions in a democracy may take more time than in a dictatorship.

**Reason (R):** In a democracy, decisions are reached by discussion and bargaining among many people and institutions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: discussing and negotiating takes time. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A democratic government is a legitimate government.

**Reason (R):** Democratic governments are always more efficient than other governments.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: it is the people's own government.
Step 2: R is false: democratic governments can be slow and inefficient; their legitimacy does not depend on efficiency. So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a democracy, citizens have the right to examine how decisions are taken.

**Reason (R):** Democratic governments hold regular elections.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: this is transparency.
Step 2: R is true, but regular elections do not explain the right to examine decision-making procedures. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Democracies have a much higher rate of economic growth than dictatorships.

**Reason (R):** Economic growth depends on several factors, such as population, the global situation and economic priorities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: on average, dictatorships have grown slightly faster; the difference is small.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Economic inequality remains high in many democracies.

**Reason (R):** Political equality through one person, one vote has not automatically produced economic equality.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: equal votes have not translated into equal incomes. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Poverty persists in many democracies.

**Reason (R):** Many democracies hold elections at regular intervals.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true, but holding elections does not explain why poverty persists. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Democracy is simply rule by majority opinion.

**Reason (R):** In a democracy, the larger group must cooperate with minorities so that government speaks for the whole people.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: democracy is not simply majority rule.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Even in a democracy, conflicts between social groups never vanish for good.

**Reason (R):** Democracies ban all social differences in order to avoid conflict.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: conflicts between groups never disappear completely; democracy manages them.
Step 2: R is false: democracies do not ban differences; they provide peaceful ways of negotiating them. So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Democracy has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged groups for equal status.

**Reason (R):** In a democracy, equality of citizens is accepted in principle, giving such claims legal and moral force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Democracy changes people from subjects into citizens.

**Reason (R):** Many citizens in democracies complain about their governments.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: people gain rights and a say in how they are governed.
Step 2: R is true, but complaints are a result of becoming citizens, not the reason for it; R does not explain A. So (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Democracies are completely free from corruption.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Corruption is found in democracies too.
Step 2: So the statement is false; but democracies let citizens expose it and vote against it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Most democracies have a good record of holding regular, free and fair elections.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Holding elections is the area where democracies do best on accountability.
Step 2: So the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Democracies have succeeded in removing poverty everywhere.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Poverty and inequality remain high in many democracies.
Step 2: So the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The fact that people complain about democracy is itself evidence of its success.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Complaints show citizens are aware, critical and free to speak.
Step 2: So the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: The openness that lets citizens check how, and by what procedure, a government decision was taken is called ___.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Openness about how decisions are taken.
Step 2: The answer is transparency.

questions.stem_md: A government that people accept as rightful because they chose it themselves is called a ___ government.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Acceptance as rightful is legitimacy.
Step 2: The answer is legitimate.

questions.stem_md: Respect for every person as an equal, which democracy protects better than other systems, is called the ___ of the individual.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Respect for each person as an equal is dignity.
Step 2: The answer is dignity.

questions.stem_md: Match each outcome of democracy with an example.

options.text_md: Accountability
Transparency
Accommodation of diversity
Dignity

match_right.text_md: Several language groups share power through regional governments
Voters remove a government that failed to control prices
A woman claims equal wages through the courts
A citizen inspects the file on how a contract was given

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Voting out a failing government: accountability (p–2).
Step 2: Inspecting a file: transparency (q–4).
Step 3: Language groups sharing power: accommodation (r–1).
Step 4: Equal wages claimed: dignity (s–3).

questions.stem_md: Match each area with the usual record of democracies.

options.text_md: Regular, free elections
Economic growth
Reducing inequality
Accommodating social diversity

match_right.text_md: About the same as dictatorships, slightly lower on average

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Elections: good record (p–2).
Step 2: Growth: about the same, slightly lower on average (q–3).
Step 3: Inequality: weak record (r–1).
Step 4: Diversity: better than non-democracies (s–4).

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the order in which a democratic government is usually held accountable for a decision.

options.text_md: Citizens form their judgement of the government's record
Citizens vote in the next election
The government takes a decision and makes information about it available
Media and opposition parties debate the decision in public

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A decision is taken and information becomes available.
Step 2: It is debated in public.
Step 3: Citizens judge the record.
Step 4: They vote.
Step 5: So the order is c, d, a, b.

marking_scheme.step: Correct order c, d, a, b

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages in the way democratic expectations usually grow.

options.text_md: They become more critical of governments that fall short
People win the right to vote
Having gained some benefits, they demand better services and more dignity
They demand that governments meet basic needs

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Political rights come first.
Step 2: Then come demands for basic needs.
Step 3: As some needs are met, expectations rise.
Step 4: Rising expectations make citizens more critical.
Step 5: So the order is b, d, c, a.

marking_scheme.step: Correct order b, d, c, a

questions.stem_md: What is meant by an accountable government? Give one way in which democracy makes government accountable.

answer.model_answer_md: An accountable government must **answer to the people** for its decisions and their results. Democracy does this through **regular, free and fair elections**, in which citizens can **remove** a government that fails them.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Meaning.
Step 2: One mechanism (elections, public debate, right to information).

questions.stem_md: What is transparency? Why is it important in a democracy?

answer.model_answer_md: Transparency is the openness that lets citizens **check how, and by what procedure,** a government decision was taken. It lets people check that **rules were followed**, which discourages **corruption** and builds **trust**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Define.
Step 2: Give its importance.

questions.stem_md: "Democratic decisions are slow, but they are better." Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Democracy relies on **discussion and negotiation**, which take **time**. But decisions reached this way have **wider support**, so they are **accepted** more readily and work better in practice.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Why slow.
Step 2: Why better.

questions.stem_md: Why is democratic government described as legitimate government, even when it is slow or inefficient?

answer.model_answer_md: It is **chosen by the people** and can be **changed by them**, so people see it as **their own** government. This acceptance, not efficiency, is what makes it **legitimate**.

questions.solution_md: Link legitimacy to popular choice, not efficiency.

marking_scheme.step: Chosen and changeable by the people
Seen as their own regardless of efficiency

questions.stem_md: Does democracy hold back economic growth? Give two points.

answer.model_answer_md: No. (i) Dictatorships have grown only **slightly faster** on average; the **difference is small**. (ii) Growth depends on many other factors, such as **population**, the **global economy** and **economic priorities**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The evidence.
Step 2: Other factors.

questions.stem_md: Give two pieces of evidence that democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequality.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) In many democracies a **small group of very rich** people earns a **large share** of income. (ii) The incomes of the **poorest** have grown slowly, and many still live in **poverty** and lack basic needs.

questions.solution_md: Two pieces of evidence: income concentration, persistent poverty.

questions.stem_md: State two conditions that democracy must meet to accommodate social diversity.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Winning a vote is **not enough**: the larger group must **cooperate with minorities** so that government speaks for the **whole people**. (ii) The majority must not be a **fixed community** defined by religion, race or language.

questions.stem_md: Explain three factors, other than the form of government, that affect a country's economic growth.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Population size**: a very large or fast-growing population must share the gains of growth. (ii) **The global economy**: world demand, prices and crises affect exports and investment. (iii) **Economic priorities and cooperation**: what a government invests in, and support from other countries, shape growth.
